one_liner: AVX2/SSE4.1/NEON RGB<->I420 converters inside a .NET OpenH264 wrapper; about 2.4x OpenCV cvtColor single-threaded, 3x multithreaded.
what_it_does: H264Sharp is a C# wrapper for Cisco OpenH264. Its native C++17 library (H264SharpNative) also holds SIMD converters between interleaved RGB/BGR/RGBA/BGRA and planar I420, plus NV12 to RGB, NV12 to I420 and a nearest-neighbour downscale. They are exposed as extern "C" functions (RGBX2YUV420(GenericImage*, YuvNative*), YUV420ToRGB(YuvNative*, GenericImage*), ConverterSetConfig) and in C# as Converter.Rgb2Yuv / Converter.Yuv2Rgb. This is a different API from cv::cvtColor and does not replace it, and the converter ships only as part of the codec DLL, not as a separate library.
how_it_is_fast: It does BT.601 limited-range conversion in 16-bit fixed point with 8-bit coefficients: 66/129/25 >> 8 for Y, the halved chroma weights 56/47/9 and 19/37/56 >> 7, and 149/128 plus x/64 terms for the inverse. One 256-bit AVX2 register therefore holds 16 pixels, while OpenCV 4.10's universal-intrinsics path widens to 32-bit lanes with 20-bit coefficients and rounding. Interleaved pixels are split with byte shuffles and blends, two rows are processed per iteration, and chroma is point-sampled from the top-left pixel of each 2x2 block (as OpenCV does) using wrap-around 16-bit arithmetic and an unsaturated pack. YUV to RGB duplicates each chroma sample with one byte shuffle and packs with saturation. Row bands go to a custom spin-wait thread pool (or PPL on Windows), with runtime dispatch on x86 (AVX2, then SSE4.1, then scalar) and NEON on arm64.
when_to_use: .NET apps (WPF, Unity, MAUI) that already use H264Sharp and OpenH264 and convert camera or screen frames between RGB and I420 every frame.
Real-time 720p/1080p capture-and-encode pipelines on x86-64 with AVX2, where frame widths are multiples of 32 (16 for the SSE and NEON paths) and heights are even.
C++ projects that want a small MIT-licensed BT.601 RGB<->I420 kernel to vendor: Rgb2YuvAVX2.cpp, Yuv2RgbAVX2.cpp and AVX2Common.h (plus the SSE/NEON variants and ThreadPool.h), built with Clang.
Video-encoder input or preview display, where values that differ from OpenCV by 1-2 code values do not matter.
when_not_to_use: BT.709/BT.2020 matrices, full-range (JPEG) YUV, 10-bit, or 4:2:2/4:4:4 layouts: only 8-bit BT.601 limited-range 4:2:0 (plus NV12 input) is implemented.

Bit-exact parity with OpenCV or libyuv, or best chroma quality. The arithmetic truncates instead of rounding, so computed from the source formulas, RGB to YUV lands 1 code value below OpenCV for about half of all inputs (mean bias about -0.5) and YUV to RGB is within +/-2. Chroma is point-sampled rather than averaged, so thin coloured edges alias.

MSVC-only or GCC-only builds without changes: the code uses Clang/GCC extensions (__attribute__((target("avx2"))), a variable-length array in ThreadPool::ForRange, #pragma clang loop), and the CMake files hard-code clang/clang++ paths.

Projects that need a maintained dependency: last commit 2025-03-14, 37 stars, open decoder-offset bugs (#20, #21), a reported AVX2 YUV-to-RGB crash on a QEMU Debian guest (#19, closed with no fix visible), and no macOS/iOS binaries (#17).

integration.form: shared lib (H264SharpNative DLL/.so with an extern "C" API, called from C# by P/Invoke; NuGet package H264Sharp); source-drop for C++ use of the converters
integration.dependencies: Cisco OpenH264 shared library for the codec part (loaded by name at runtime); the converter files need only the repo's ThreadPool.h, Logger and pch headers; the Windows build links 'synchronization' and can use PPL (concurrency::parallel_for)
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 with Clang (CMakeLists hard-codes clang/clang++, CMakePresets uses LLVM clang++ on Windows, the vcxproj uses ClangCL); the C# wrapper targets .NET Standard and the benchmark targets net6.0
integration.platforms: x86/x86-64 (runtime dispatch: AVX2, SSE4.1, scalar), arm64 NEON, other ARM scalar; prebuilt binaries for Windows, Linux and Android, none for macOS/iOS
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the converter settings are one process-wide static (Converter::Config, changed by SetConfig) and multithreaded conversions share one static thread pool, so set the config once before converting from several threads

gotchas: RGBX2YUV420 writes one contiguous I420 buffer starting at to->Y, with Y stride equal to the width and U then V directly after it; it ignores the U/V pointers and strides in YuvNative. YUV420ToRGB does honour strides.

Width decides the path without telling you: AVX2 needs width % 32 == 0 and SSE/NEON need % 16, otherwise the scalar code runs. Images under 640x480 always run on one thread. With the custom pool, each worker needs at least 245,760 pixels (128 rows at 1080p), so 1080p uses at most 8 workers however many threads you request.
The SIMD loops step two rows at a time and always touch row y+1, with no tail handling, so an odd height reads and writes one row past the planes (found in the source, not reported in any issue).

Rgb2Yuv.cpp contains a 2x2-averaging chroma routine, but nothing calls it: the scalar, SSE, AVX2 and NEON paths all point-sample chroma. Release v1.6.0 notes a 'YUV luminance overflow' fix, and the README does not say which version produced its benchmark tables.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it when you are already in .NET with OpenH264 and want RGB<->I420 at about 2.4-3x OpenCV with matched threads. For C++ code, libyuv (the incumbent, with many more formats and matrices) or the smaller xxYUV and descampsa/yuv2rgb are easier to adopt, and sparkyuv or yuvutils-rs cover more matrices and bit depths.
verified_claims_summary: README tables, measured on 1080p with 5000 iterations; each iteration is one YUV420-to-RGB plus one RGB-to-YUV420 call from C#, with matched thread counts. The OpenCV side is 4.10 through the OpenCvSharp4 4.10.0.20241108 Windows runtime; the H264Sharp side is a prebuilt native DLL whose compiler and flags are not stated. Ryzen 7 3700X: 4899 vs 11919 ms on one thread (2.43x) and 822 vs 2543 ms on 8 threads (3.09x). i7-10600U: 6010 vs 11719 ms (1.95x). Both libraries point-sample chroma, so they do the same work. H264Sharp computes in truncating 16-bit lanes where OpenCV uses rounded 32-bit lanes (outputs within 1-2 code values, derived from the source formulas), and its 16-thread row used at most 8 workers.
